updates.note: Introduced as a Calallen teacher setting up her classroom; keeps a yellow storm-closure checklist by her classroom door; wants "one text, one time, from one place" for closure notices; lives a short drive from the O.N. Stevens plant on the Nueces River.

Introduced on the first day of school: home health aide, 38, three children, youngest is 6; the two older children ride the school bus; she rides city buses between clients; says "Mi carro es el bus"; has not yet registered for evacuation assistance ("I sign up my clients. I'm always signing up somebody else").
Quoted on the evacuation-ride gap: "Everybody is counting on somebody with a car, and the people with cars are the first ones to leave."
Quoted on the anchorage as the export system's buffer: "When everything's moving, nobody notices it."

Profiled at the Aransas Pass harbor; keeps a spiral notebook of catch and fuel for every trip; father shrimped the same bays; says "Fair doesn't pay for diesel"; watches September skies more than his nets.

Introduced as a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer, 42, who films the night sky from his backyard on clear nights and logs time, direction and what he thinks each light was; writes "unknown" when unsure; says "I'd rather say 'I don't know' than say something that isn't true."
Quoted on late-August loadings: "The pipes are full and the docks are busy"; flags freight and the hurricane season as the two September variables.
Explained the seasonal outlook: "An outlook is a weather forecast for the whole ocean, not for your street"; urged residents to make sure they have a plan.

Profiled: 59, keeps a penciled binder list of neighbors without cars or working phones; helps people register through 2-1-1; keeps water and canned goods in a fellowship hall storage closet; says "Nobody should have to be brave because they're poor."

Profiled at Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties: 64, rode out two hurricanes on the island and does not recommend it ("The first time I thought I was brave. The second time I knew better"); keeps plywood cut and labeled in the back; strong summer, "more than last year, less than I'd like."

Introduced on his North Beach porch: 67, retired welder, notices tides and wind; says his storm plan is "water, a radio and a ladder"; teased a neighbor's sprinkler during the water-conservation push.
Explained forecast products: "Ignore the line. Watch the whole cone, and then look past it"; on surge: "Wind you can hide from in a sturdy building. Water you can't."
Quoted on the relief supply chain from the neighborhood level: "The big warehouses are for the region. My closet is for the block."
Quoted on the August monthly high: "Half of the country's crude exports through one channel is a remarkable concentration. It's efficient right up until something interrupts it."
Quoted in the Ledger on concentration risk: "One channel is a strength until it's the only thing anybody's talking about."

Quoted as a home health aide on clients who cannot evacuate on their own ("Ay, you think I'm going to carry them to the bus?"); has helped clients register with STEAR; still has not registered her own family ("This week. Lo prometo.").
Arc beat: wrote the Ledger's Rafael formation story.
On Rafael's formation: "This is the time to pay attention, not the time to panic... The cone is wide for a reason."
On Rafael's formation: "It's a long way from a tropical storm in the Gulf to a closed channel... people don't wait for the closure to start asking questions."
Labor Day weekend: says everyone is a meteorologist; "watch the birds and watch the TV, and believe the TV"; plywood cut in May stays in the back for now; ran out of ice twice.
Began calling the neighbors on her list after Rafael formed: medicine, a ride, 2-1-1 registration, a charged phone; says "The storm doesn't know who has a car. But we do."
Got a call from Pastor Whitfield; still had not registered for an evacuation ride ("Pastora, I know, I know. This week. For real this time.").
On rain bands: "When the ground is already full, rain has nowhere to go but the streets and the rivers... (rain-band quote removed in hardening; see story)

Started a neighbors' group text sharing the online Nueces River gauge reading at Calallen; frustrated that "a number on a website isn't a plan" and wants officials to say what the river means for residents.
Explained saturated ground on Coastline: "Rain on saturated ground is like pouring water into a full glass."
On Rafael becoming a hurricane: "Warm water is fuel, and Rafael is sitting on a lot of it... Do the things you'd do in three days, today."
Arc beat, forecast cone: (watch quote removed in hardening; see story)
Under the forecast cone: no evacuation order yet; urged residents without cars to call 2-1-1 now; said shelters will be inland and locations announced before anyone is asked to go.

Confirmed 40 relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider; "The whole game is pre-positioning"; "Weather sets the schedule. We just hold the bookings"; acknowledged the ship would wait like everyone else if the channel closes.
Registered her family for an evacuation ride through 2-1-1 on the day of the forecast cone ("Okay, Rosa, ya"); packing one bag per person; worried about her home health clients.
"If you don't have a way out, we need to know before the order, not after. We plan the buses off that list."
Arc beat: reported the aircraft evacuation to NAS JRB Fort Worth.
Confirmed training aircraft flown to NAS JRB Fort Worth: "a precaution... what we plan and train for every season."
Confirmed depot halted work and secured helicopters; workforce sent home to care for families: "We'll tell them when it's time to come back."
Arc beat: published the families' evacuation guide special edition.
Told families to follow command and county guidance and keep NFAAS information current.
To depot employees: "Take care of your families first. Keep your phone on, and watch for word from your supervisor."
To the Ledger: "When we're ready to bring people back, they'll hear it from us first"; would not speculate on how long work would be paused.
Seen buying batteries and water jugs as the forecast cone covered the city: "I've done this more times than these kids have had birthdays."
Arc beat: wrote the Ledger's evacuation-zone explainer.
Arc beat, mandatory evacuation: "If you're in a surge zone, this isn't advice anymore. It's an order"; told residents who called for a ride to stay by the phone with one bag per person.
"We are working through the list as fast as we can. If you're waiting on a bus, stay where we can find you."
Boarded up the bait shop with his labeled plywood under the evacuation order; would not say whether he would ride out a third storm on the island ("Ask me tomorrow").
Doubled the lines on his shrimp boat in the Aransas Pass harbor; planned to leave once the boat was secured ("Boat I can fix. Me, not so easy").
Cut Sunday service short and turned the fellowship hall into a place to charge phones and make calls for neighbors waiting on county buses; working down her list; "I'll go when my list is done."
To Coastline: "We are getting to people as fast as we can. If you're waiting, stay where we can find you."
Arc beat, life-threatening surge warning: "Nine to 12 feet of water is not a flood you wade through... If you've been told to leave, leave now. Not after lunch."
Hurricane warning day: "This is the last good window. When the wind picks up, we can't send a bus into it."
Filed the national hurricane-warning story from Corpus Christi.
Hurricane warning day: "Our aircraft are safe in Fort Worth, and our focus now is our people"; aircraft return after the station is assessed.
"The hangars are locked down and our folks are with their families. That's exactly where we want them tonight."
Said nothing has changed on the brigade beyond the postponement: "When the port is ready, we'll be ready."
Told Harborline 6 by phone he was staying in his North Beach home through the storm despite the mandatory evacuation: "I heard them. I'm still here."
